paragraphs.heading: What a vent is
paragraphs.text: A hydrothermal vent is a crack in the seabed where water heated by the Earth's inner heat flows out. Vents exist because our planet is geologically active and holds large amounts of water, both on its surface and inside its crust. They are common near volcanoes, at hotspots, in ocean basins, and at mid-ocean ridges where tectonic plates pull apart.

paragraphs.heading: Where the water comes from
paragraphs.text: In the deep ocean, vents typically line the mid-ocean ridges, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the East Pacific Rise among them, where two plates separate and fresh crust forms. Most of the water they release is seawater drawn into the system near the volcano through faults, porous sediment or volcanic rock. A little extra water is released by the magma welling up below.

paragraphs.heading: Very hot, but not boiling
paragraphs.text: The sea around deep vents sits near 2 °C, but vent water emerges at temperatures from 60 °C to as much as 464 °C. Because the water pressure at these depths is so high, the water can stay liquid, or it can become a supercritical fluid, a state with properties between those of a gas and a liquid. Pure water reaches this critical point at 375 °C and 218 atmospheres. Salt pushes the point higher: for seawater it is 407 °C and 298.5 bars, the pressure at roughly 2,960 m below sea level.

paragraphs.heading: Supercritical vents
paragraphs.text: Supercritical venting has been seen at several sites. At Beebe, in the Cayman Trough, the deepest known vent site at about 5,000 m down, fluid has vented steadily in this state at 401 °C. Another site, Turtle Pits, vented low-salt fluid at 407 °C, above the critical point for that saltiness. Scientists do not yet know whether this matters for how vent water circulates, how mineral deposits build, the flow of chemicals into the sea, or living things.

paragraphs.heading: Chimneys and smokers
paragraphs.text: Some vents build roughly cylindrical chimneys. Minerals dissolved in the hot fluid come out as particles when it meets the near-freezing sea, and those particles stack up. Growth of about 30 cm a day has been recorded, and some chimneys stand 60 m tall. Under the sea, vents may form black smokers or white smokers, which carry a wide range of elements into the world's oceans.

paragraphs.heading: Life around the vents
paragraphs.text: Compared with most of the deep sea, vent areas are rich in life, often whole communities that run on chemicals dissolved in the vent fluid. Bacteria and archaea living there form the base of the food chain, feeding giant tube worms, clams, limpets and shrimp. Vents have been proposed as an important factor in how life began and how early life survived. Separately, their conditions have been shown to support making molecules important to life. Active vents are also thought to exist beyond Earth, on Europa, a moon of Jupiter, and Enceladus, a moon of Saturn.
